3 Layers, 1 Stack
Beck breaks the industry into three tiers, and the biggest one sits furthest from the launchpad.

“Rockets, that’s about a $10 or $20 billion industry. Spacecraft, the tools in space to provide services, $20 to $30 billion. And then the reason why you do all of those things are applications in space,” he said.

He also joked about a branding problem. “I probably shouldn’t have called it Rocket Lab. I should have called it Space Lab. The rocket always steals the show because it’s this big roaring stick in the sky.”

The Iridium Piece

The $8 billion cash-and-stock purchase of Iridium supplies the missing top layer. Rocket Lab picks up a 66-satellite low-Earth-orbit network, globally coordinated L-band spectrum and more than 2.5 million largely enterprise and government subscribers.
Rocket Lab told Reuters the deal is “one of the most transformative deals in the space industry,” creating “a fully-integrated, self-launching, tier-1 space power.”
Beck’s argument is speed: building that network in-house would have taken years and billions.

Why Traders Care

The Rocket Lab-SpaceX comparison is structural. Owning launch, manufacturing and the constellation removes third-party launch costs and adds recurring service revenue to an otherwise capital-hungry space business. Iridium generated $871.7 million in 2025 revenue, compared with Rocket Lab’s $602 million.
Upcoming catalysts include FCC consent to transfer control of licenses to Rocket Lab and Neutron’s debut flight, expected in the fourth quarter of 2026.

Beck’s closing point explains the end market. “Space is kinda weird that it’s hidden infrastructure. You don’t drive past it every day, so you don’t see it. But everybody interfaces with space every single day, whether you realize it or not.”
